query: For W–Cu metal-matrix composites used in heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications, what single intervention could increase thermal conductivity while retaining mechanical durability and irradiation resistance? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an otherwise comparable W–Cu composite, defines the application conditions under which it should hold, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the sintering temperature during processing will promote enhanced copper phase slip and rearrangement to form a more continuous three‐dimensional copper network in the W–Cu composite, thereby raising its thermal conductivity while retaining its mechanical durability and irradiation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: A chemically plated tungsten–copper composite powder (e.g., W–20Cu) with a partially interconnected, but not fully optimized, copper network.
generation.intervention: Increase the sintering temperature to an optimized higher range (but below the threshold where excessive copper evaporation or closed-porosity forms) during heat-treatment.
generation.conditions: Processing should occur under inert/reducing atmosphere with controlled sintering time to balance densification and avoid copper over-evaporation, ensuring that the tungsten skeleton remains intact.
generation.structural_mediator: A denser and more uniform three-dimensional copper network that bridges tungsten particles.
generation.mechanism: A higher sintering temperature enhances the slip and diffusion of liquid-phase copper. This drives its redistribution and rearrangement around tungsten particles, reducing interfacial defects. The improved copper network provides more efficient electron and phonon pathways for heat transport while the tungsten matrix maintains structural integrity and irradiation resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline composite sintered at a lower temperature, the composite processed at the optimized higher temperature will show increased thermal conductivity (by an estimated several percentage points, within the uncertainty range) with mechanical strength and irradiation resistance remaining within acceptable limits.
generation.baseline: A W–Cu composite produced using conventional lower sintering temperatures where the copper network is less continuous and densification is lower.
generation.boundary: If sintering temperatures exceed the optimal range, excessive copper evaporation and pore formation may occur, potentially degrading mechanical properties and irradiation resistance.
generation.uncertainty: The precise temperature window and extent of thermal conductivity improvement are not fully quantified, and long-term irradiation performance under actual reactor conditions requires further validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of chemically plated W–20Cu composite powders. Sinter one batch at a conventional lower temperature and the other at the optimized higher temperature (carefully chosen to avoid excessive copper loss). Characterize both batches for density, microstructure (via SEM/EDS to check copper network continuity), thermal conductivity, mechanical properties (e.g., hardness, yield strength), and perform a controlled irradiation test that simulates fusion reactor conditions.
measurements: Thermal conductivity (using laser flash analysis or comparable method)
Mechanical properties (Vickers hardness, compressive yield strength)
Microstructural analysis (SEM, EDS for copper network connectivity; porosity assessment)
Irradiation resistance (post-irradiation characterization for defect formation and phase stability)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the composite sintered at the higher temperature does not demonstrate a statistically significant increase in thermal conductivity compared to the baseline, or if its mechanical durability and irradiation resistance are degraded (e.g., increased porosity, reduced strength, or enhanced radiation-induced defect formation), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.3. Effect of Sintering Time on the Microstructure of Alloys
cited_evidence.text: Figure 8 reveals the microstructure of W-20Cu composite after sintering the W-20Cu specimens at 1350 °C for 60, 120 and 180 min, respectively, where the grey tissue is the skeleton-like tungsten phase, and the light black tissue is the adherent phase copper at its periphery. A small number of tiny pores can be observed in Figure 8b1, and the copper phase is distributed in the interstices of tungsten particles. With the increasing sintering time, the pore size distribution first becomes more obvious and then decreases, which is due to the fact that in the process of high-temperature liquid-phase sintering, the wettability between the tungsten and copper is not very good at 1350 °C [,,,] and the liquid-phase copper will produce evaporation loss after generation. At the same time, due to the incomplete liquid-phase wettability, the interfacial energy of the solid–solid interface is lower than that of the solid–liquid interface, and solid particles come in contact with each other, making the copper melt permeation volume higher, so that the amount of copper melt penetration is reduced, part of the copper had to overflow.
